READING 3
BENCHMARKING RETURNS
MODULE 3.1: TIME-WEIGHTED AND MONEY-
WEIGHTED RETURNS
LOS 3.a: Calculate and compare money-weighted and time-weighted rates
of return.
The money-weighted return (or dollar-weighted return) applies the concept of
the internal rate of return (IRR) to investment portfolios. An IRR is the
interest rate at which a series of cash inflows and outflows sum to zero when
discounted to their present value. That is, they have a net present value (NPV)
of zero. The IRR and NPV are built-in functions on financial calculators that
CFA Institute permits candidates to use for the exam.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
We have provided an online video in our Resource Library on how to
use the TI calculator. You can view it by logging in to your account at
www.schweser.com.
The money-weighted rate of return is defined as the IRR on a portfolio,
considering all cash inflows and outflows. The beginning value of the account is
an inflow, as are all deposits into the account. All withdrawals from the account
are outflows, as is the ending value.
EXAMPLE: Money-weighted rate of return
Assume an investor buys a share of stock for $100 at t = 0. The share pays a $2
cash dividend during the year, and the investor does not reinvest the dividend.
At t = 1 (the end of the first year and the beginning of the second), she buys an
additional share for $120. The shares pay another cash dividend of $2 per share
during the year, and again, the investor does not reinvest the dividends. At t = 2

(the end of Year 2), the investor sells both shares for $130 each. What is the
money-weighted rate of return?
Answer:
The intuition, here, is that we deposited $100 into the account at t = 0, then
added $118 to the account at t = 1 (which, with the $2 dividend, funded the
purchase of one more share at $120), and ended with a total value of $264.
To compute this value with a financial calculator, use these net cash flows and
follow the procedure(s) described to calculate the IRR:
net cash flows: CF0 = +100; CF1 = +120 − 2 = +118;
CF2 = −260 + −4 = −264

The keystrokes to calculate the money-weighted return with the TI Business
Analyst II Plus® are as follows. Note that the values for F01, F02, and so on
are all equal to 1.
The money-weighted rate of return for this problem is 13.86%.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
In the preceding example, we entered the flows into the account as a
positive and the ending value as a negative (the investor could withdraw
this amount from the account). Note that there is no difference in the
solution if we enter the cash flows into the account as negative values
(out of the investor’s pocket) and the ending value as a positive value
(into the investor’s pocket). If payments into the account and payments
out of the account (including the ending value) are entered with
opposite signs, the computed IRR will be correct.
We also assumed the investor did not reinvest the cash dividends. In the
Equities topic area, we will examine the effect of reinvested dividends
on an investor’s return.
Time-weighted return measures compound growth and is the rate at which $1
compounds over a specified performance horizon. Time-weighting is the process
of averaging a set of values over time. The annual time-weighted return for an
investment may be computed by performing the following steps:
Step 1:    Value the portfolio immediately preceding significant additions or
withdrawals. Form subperiods over the evaluation period that correspond
to the dates of deposits and withdrawals.
Step 2:    Compute the holding period return (HPR) of the portfolio for each
subperiod.
Step 3:    Compute the product of (1 + HPR) for each subperiod to obtain a total
return for the entire measurement period [i.e., (1 + HPR1) × (1 + HPR2)

. . . (1 + HPRn)] − 1. If the total investment period is greater than one
year, you must take the geometric mean of the measurement period
return, based on the number of years in the measurement period, to find
the annual time-weighted rate of return.
EXAMPLE: Time-weighted rate of return
An investor purchases a share of stock at t = 0 for $100. At the end of the year,
t = 1, the investor buys another share of the same stock for $120. At the end of
Year 2, the investor sells both shares for $130 each. At the end of both Years 1
and 2, the stock paid a $2 per share dividend. What is the annual time-
weighted rate of return for this investment? (This is the same investment as the
preceding example.)
Answer:
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
The 0.5 exponent is the reciprocal of the number of years in the holding
period (1 / 2 = 0.5). The number of years is not necessarily the same as
the number of subperiods being considered during the overall holding
period.

Unlike the money-weighted rate of return, the time-weighted rate of return is not
affected by the timing of cash inflows and outflows. In the investment
management industry, time-weighted return is the preferred method of
performance measurement because portfolio managers typically do not control
the timing of deposits to and withdrawals from the accounts they manage.
In the preceding examples, the time-weighted rate of return for the portfolio was
15.84%, while the money-weighted rate of return for the same portfolio was
13.86%. The results are different because the money-weighted rate of return
gave a larger weight to the Year 2 HPR, which was 10%, versus the 22% HPR
for Year 1. This is because there was more money in the account at the beginning
of the second period.
If funds are contributed to an investment portfolio just before a period of
relatively poor portfolio performance, the money-weighted rate of return will
tend to be lower than the time-weighted rate of return. On the other hand, if
funds are contributed to a portfolio at a favorable time (just before a period of
relatively high returns), the money-weighted rate of return will be higher than
the time-weighted rate of return. The use of the time-weighted return removes
these distortions, so it provides a better measure of a manager’s ability to select
investments over the period. If the manager has complete control over money
flows into and out of an account, the money-weighted rate of return would be the
more appropriate performance measure.
CFA Institute has developed Global Investment Performance Standards
(GIPS), a voluntary set of performance presentation guidelines for investment
management firms. Firms that claim compliance with GIPS must use time-
weighted returns to present investment performance, except under a specific set
of conditions that make money-weighted returns more appropriate. These
include the investment manager controlling cash flows into the portfolio, in
addition to the portfolio being closed end, having a fixed life, having committed
capital from investors that the manager can call on demand, or consisting largely
of illiquid investments.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
GIPS are addressed in detail in the Level III CFA curriculum.
MODULE QUIZ 3.1
1. An investor buys a share of stock for $40, buys another share of the same stock for $50
at the beginning of the next period, and sells both shares for $60 each at the end of that

period. The stock pays a dividend of $1 per share at the end of each period, and the
investor does not reinvest the dividends. The periodic money-weighted rate of return on
the investment is closest to:
A. 22.2%.
B. 23.0%.
C. 23.8%.
2. An investor buys a share of stock for $40, buys another share of the same stock for $50
at the beginning of the next period, and sells both shares for $60 each at the end of that
period. The stock pays a dividend of $1 per share at the end of each period, and the
investor does not reinvest the dividends. The time-weighted rate of return on the
investment for the period is closest to:
A. 24.7%.
B. 25.7%.
C. 26.8%.
MODULE 3.2: SECURITY MARKET INDEXES
LOS 3.b: Describe the choices and the implications of the different
weighting methods used in index construction and management, and
calculate, interpret, and explain the value and the returns of an index.
A security market index is used to represent the performance of an asset class,
security market, or segment of a market. They are usually created as portfolios
of individual securities, which are referred to as the constituent securities of the
index. An index has a numerical value that is calculated from the market prices
(actual when available, or estimated) of its constituent securities at a point in
time. An index return is the percentage change in the index’s value over a period.
An index return may be calculated using a price index or a return index. A
price index uses only the prices of the constituent securities in the return
calculation. A rate of return that is calculated based on a price index is referred
to as a price return.
A return index includes both prices and income from the constituent securities. A
rate of return that is calculated based on a return index is called a total return. If
the assets in an index produce interim cash flows such as dividends or interest
payments, the total return will be greater than the price return.
Once returns are calculated for each period, they then can be compounded
together to arrive at the return for the measurement period:

For example, if the returns for the first two periods were 0.50% and 1.04%, they
would be geometrically linked to produce 1.55%:
RP = (1 + RS1)(1 + RS2) − 1 = (1.005)(1.0104) − 1 = 0.0155, or 1.55%
If the starting index value is 100, its value after two periods would be 100 ×
1.0155 = 101.55.
We can describe a process for constructing, calculating, and maintaining a
security market index using the following five steps:
Step 1:    Objective of the index. Specify the security market or sector the index
will measure.
Step 2:    Constituent securities. Define the criteria and select securities that meet
them.
Step 3:    Weighting method. Weighting schemes include price weighting, equal
weighting, market capitalization weighting, float-adjusted market
capitalization weighting, and fundamental weighting.
Step 4:    Calculations. Determine the index value on an initial date and on
subsequent dates.
Step 5:    Maintenance. Over time, it may become necessary to rebalance or
reconstitute an index (e.g., to reflect corporate actions such as mergers or
bankruptcies), and to re-evaluate the security selection criteria and the
index construction process.
Price Weighting
A price-weighted index is essentially an arithmetic average of the prices of the
securities included in the index, with its denominator adjusted for changes in the
composition of the index over time—such that the index value is unaffected by
such changes. The denominator is adjusted when securities are added or deleted
from the index, and when corporate actions change the proportion of a company
that one share represents. These actions include stock splits, in which one share
becomes a larger number of shares (e.g., a 2-for-1 stock split means one share

becomes two shares, but each of those shares represents half as much ownership
of the company as one share represented before the split); reverse stock splits,
in which some number of shares become one share; and stock dividends, which
are similar to stock splits except that they are stated as a percentage (e.g., a 10%
stock dividend means one share becomes 1.1 shares).
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
It is crucial to distinguish between stock dividends and cash dividends.
A cash dividend pays part of a company’s earnings to shareholders. A
stock dividend does not pay cash or change a shareholder’s ownership
position; like a stock split, it merely changes what one share represents.
We will examine these transactions with shareholders in more detail in
the Equities topic area, as well as in Financial Statement Analysis when
we calculate earnings per share.

EXAMPLE: Adjusting a price-weighted index for stock splits
Stock A has a price of $5, Stock B has a price of $25, and Stock C has a price
of $90. The value of a price-weighted index of these three stocks is (5 + 25 +
90) / 1.2 = 100. If Stock C splits 2-for-1, effective on the next day, what is the
new denominator for the index?
Answer:
The effect of the split on the price of Stock C, in the absence of any change
from the price at the end of Day 1, would be to reduce it to $90 / 2 = $45. The
index denominator will be adjusted so that the index value would remain at
100 if there were no changes in the stock prices, other than to adjust for the
split. The new denominator, D, must satisfy (5 + 25 + 45) / D = 100 and equals
0.75.
The returns on a price-weighted index could be matched by purchasing an equal
number of shares of each stock represented in the index.
The advantage of a price-weighted index is that its computation is simple. One
disadvantage is that a given percentage change in the price of a higher-priced
stock has a greater impact on the index’s value than does an equal percentage
change in the price of a lower-priced stock. Put another way, higher-priced
stocks have more weight in the calculation of a price-weighted index.
Additionally, the price of a single share does not indicate the market value of a
company, because companies may have widely different numbers of shares
outstanding. For this reason, a price-weighted index is typically a suitable
benchmark only for a portfolio that is affected disproportionately by price
changes of specific securities.
Two major price-weighted indexes are the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA)
and the Nikkei Stock Average (Nikkei 225). The DJIA is a price-weighted index
based on 30 US stocks. The Nikkei is constructed from the prices of 225 stocks
that trade in the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
Equal Weighting

An equal-weighted index places an equal weight on the returns of all index
stocks, regardless of their prices or market values. A $2 change in the price of a
$20 stock has the same effect on the index as a $30 change in the price of a $300
stock, regardless of the size of the company. Because price changes of an index’s
constituent securities cause their weights in the index to drift, maintaining an
equal-weighted index requires frequent rebalancing.
The following example illustrates how an equal-weighted index is assigned a
value at inception and how price changes affect the index.
EXAMPLE: Equal-weighted index
Calculate the equal-weighted index value for the three stocks described in the
following table, assuming an initial index value of 100.
Equal-Weighted Index Data
Answer:
Initial Value
At inception, each stock in the index is assigned an equal reference value. The
index includes the number of shares of each stock that is required to equal that
reference value. Here, we will use 5,200 as the reference value (the value
chosen is arbitrary).
Stock A: 5,200 / $12 = 433.33 shares
Stock B: 5,200 / $52 = 100 shares
Stock C: 5,200 / $38 = 136.84 shares
The aggregate reference value is 3 × 5,200 = 15,600. To set the initial index
value to 100, we use a divisor of 156.

Current Value
Stock A: 433.33 shares × $15 = 6,500.0
Stock B: 100 shares × $48 = 4,800.0
Stock C: 136.84 shares × $45 = 6,158.0
Aggregate reference value = 6,500.0 + 4,800.0 + 6,158.0 = 17,458.0
Index value = 17,458.0 / 156 = 111.9
The index value increased by 11.9%. Notice that this equals the arithmetic
average of the percentage changes in the stocks’ prices:
Thus, each stock’s performance had an equal influence on the index’s
performance. For this to remain true going forward, however, the index would
need to be rebalanced such that each stock’s reference value was once again
equal.
One complication with an equal-weighted index return is that a matching
portfolio would have to be adjusted periodically (rebalanced) as prices change so
that the values of all security positions are made equal each period. The portfolio

rebalancing required to match the performance of an equal-weighted index
creates high transactions costs that decrease portfolio returns.
An equal-weighted index can be a suitable benchmark for an investment strategy
that is designed to limit exposure to companies with the largest market
capitalizations.
The Value Line Composite Average and the Financial Times Ordinary Share
Index are well-known examples of equal-weighted indexes.
Market Capitalization Weighting
A market-capitalization-weighted index (or value-weighted index) has
weights based on the market capitalization of each index stock (current stock
price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding) as a proportion of the total
market capitalization of all the stocks in the index. This weighting method more
closely represents changes in aggregate investor wealth than price weighting.
Because the weight of an index stock is based on a company’s total market
value, a market-capitalization-weighted index does not need to be adjusted for a
stock split or a stock dividend, as those transactions do not change the value of a
company. (The divisor does need to be adjusted when an index’s components
change.)
A market-capitalization-weighted index is calculated by summing the total value
of all the stocks in the index. This sum is then divided by a divisor that gives the
index its base period value (typically 100 or 1,000).
EXAMPLE: Market-capitalization-weighted index
In its base period on December 31, the total market value of an index portfolio
is $80 million. One month later, on January 31, the market value of the
portfolio is $95 million. If the base period index value is 100, calculate the
index value on January 31.
Answer:
To set the base-year index to 100, the divisor is 80 million / 100 = 800,000.

A market-capitalization-weighted index return can be matched with a portfolio in
which the allocation to each security is the same as the proportion of that
security’s market capitalization to that of all the securities in the index.

An alternative to using a firm’s market capitalization to calculate its weight is to
use its market float. A firm’s market float is the total value of the shares that are
actually available to the investing public. This excludes the value of shares held
by strategic stockholders because they are unlikely to sell their shares. Market
float is often calculated also excluding shares held by corporations or
governments. A market float calculation that excludes shares not available to
foreign buyers is referred to as free float. The point of using a market float
measure is to better match the index weights of stocks to their proportions of the
total value of all the shares of index stocks that are available to investors.
A float-adjusted market-capitalization-weighted index is constructed like a
market-capitalization-weighted index. The weights, however, are based on the
proportionate value of each firm’s shares available to investors to the total
market value of the shares of index stocks available to investors. Firms with
relatively large percentages of their shares held by controlling stockholders will
have less weight than they have in an unadjusted market-capitalization index.
Advantages of market-capitalization-weighted indexes of either type are that
index security weights represent proportions of total market value; that they tend
to have infrequent turnover of their constituent securities; and that rebalancing
happens automatically for a portfolio that tracks such an index. Their primary
disadvantage is that the relative impact of a stock’s return on the index increases
as its price rises and decreases as its price falls. This means that stocks that are
possibly overvalued are given disproportionately high weights in the index, and
stocks that are possibly undervalued are given disproportionately low weights.
A market-capitalization-weighted index is typically a suitable benchmark for a
passive investment strategy that is designed to earn the market rate of return. The
Standard and Poor’s 500 (S&P 500) Index Composite is an example of a market-
capitalization-weighted index.

Fundamental Weighting
An index that uses fundamental weighting uses weights based on firm
fundamentals, such as earnings, dividends, or cash flow. In contrast to market
capitalization index weights, these weights are unaffected by the share prices of
the index stocks (although related to them over the long term). Fundamental
weights can be based on a single measure or some combination of fundamental
measures. A fundamental-weighted index can be used as a performance
benchmark for an active fund manager who believes changes in fundamental
factors drive future stock performance and cause individual firms’ securities to
outperform or underperform the market.
An advantage of a fundamental-weighted index is that it focuses on factors
beyond share prices and market capitalization. A disadvantage is that a
fundamental-weighted index may exclude non-dividend-paying stocks or firms
that do not currently have positive earnings, which may bias the index toward or
away from some market sectors. A fundamental-weighted index typically has a
value tilt, overweighting firms with high value-based metrics such as book-to-
market ratios or earnings yields. Thus, it can be a suitable benchmark for
investors who are employing value-driven strategies.
Rebalancing and Reconstitution of an Index

Rebalancing refers to adjusting the weights of securities in a portfolio to their
target weights after price changes have affected the weights. For index
calculations, rebalancing to target weights on the index securities is done on a
periodic basis, usually quarterly. Because the weights in price- and value-
weighted indexes (portfolios) are adjusted to their correct values by changes in
prices, rebalancing is an issue primarily for equal-weighted and fundamental-
weighted indexes.
As noted previously, the weights on security returns in an (initially) equal-
weighted portfolio do not remain equal as securities prices change over time.
Therefore, rebalancing the portfolio at the end of each period used to calculate
index returns is necessary for the portfolio return to match the index return. For a
portfolio that tracks an equal-weighted index, this tends to result in selling stocks
that have increased in value and buying stocks that have decreased in value—
both of which are contrary to a trend-following strategy, which would instead
“cut losses short and let profits run.”

Index reconstitution refers to periodically adding and deleting securities that
make up an index. Securities are deleted if they no longer meet the index criteria
(e.g., a company in the S&P 500 Index may fall out of the top 500 companies by
market capitalization) and are replaced by other securities that do. Indexes are
also reconstituted to reflect corporate events, such as bankruptcy or delisting of
index firms. The index’s divisor is adjusted at the date of the reconstitution to
keep the index constant.
When a security is added to an index, its price tends to rise as portfolio managers
who are seeking to track that index in a portfolio buy the security. The prices of
deleted securities tend to fall as portfolio managers sell them. Additions and
deletions also require that the weights on the returns of other index stocks be
adjusted to conform to the desired weighting scheme.

KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 3.a
The money-weighted rate of return is the IRR calculated using periodic cash
flows into and out of an account and is the discount rate that makes the present
value of cash inflows equal to the present value of cash outflows.
The time-weighted rate of return measures compound growth and is the rate at
which money compounds over a specified performance horizon.

If funds are added to a portfolio just before a period of poor performance, the
money-weighted return will be lower than the time-weighted return. If funds are
added just before a period of high returns, the money-weighted return will be
higher than the time-weighted return.
The time-weighted return is the preferred measure of a manager’s ability to
select investments. If the manager controls the money flows into and out of an
account, the money-weighted return is the more appropriate performance
measure.
LOS 3.b
A security market index represents the performance of an asset class, security
market, or segment of a market. The performance of the market or segment over
a period is represented by the percentage change in (i.e., the return on) the value
of the index.
A price index uses only the prices of the constituent securities in the return
calculation. The rate of return is called a price return. A total return index uses
both the price of and the income from the index securities in the return
calculation. The rate of return is called a total return.
Constructing, calculating, and managing an index involves five steps:
Step 1:    State the objective and specify the market or sector.
Step 2:    Select the constituent securities.
Step 3:    Determine the weighting method.
Step 4:    Calculate the index value on the initial date and subsequent dates.
Step 5:    Rebalance and reconstitute the index when needed and evaluate the
construction and selection process.
A price-weighted index is an arithmetic mean of the prices of the index
securities. Its divisor must be adjusted for stock splits and changes in the
composition of the index over time. Higher-priced stocks have more weight in
the returns of a price-weighted index than lower-priced stocks.
An equal-weighted index places an equal weight on the returns of all index
stocks, regardless of their prices or market values. Because price changes of an
index’s constituent securities cause their weights in the index to drift,
maintaining an equal-weighted index requires frequent rebalancing.

A market-capitalization-weighted index gives each constituent security a weight
equal to its proportion of the total market value of all securities in the index.
Market capitalization can be adjusted for a security’s market float or free float to
reflect the fact that not all outstanding shares are available for purchase.
A fundamental-weighted index uses weights that are independent of security
prices, such as company earnings, revenue, assets, or cash flow.
Index providers periodically rebalance the weights of the constituent securities.
This is most important for equal-weighted and fundamental-weighted indexes.
Reconstitution refers to changing the securities that are included in an index.
This is necessary when securities mature, or when they no longer have the
required characteristics to be included.
